alt: The partly built tree with one skipped edge at a time. The skipped edge is marked, and the path of accepted edges that already joins its two ends is highlighted, showing that every edge on that path costs no more than the skipped one.

steps.caption: Kruskal's algorithm builds the tree edge by edge. Each step below stops at an edge it skips, with the tree built so far marked. A skipped edge's ends are already joined by accepted edges, so it would close a cycle.
Edge 0-3 costs 6, but the tree already joins 0 to 3 through 0-1 (5), 1-2 (3), 2-3 (4). Every one of those edges costs at most 6, so 0-3 would only add a dearer way round a loop. Skip it.
Edge 1-4 costs 7, but the tree already joins 1 to 4 through 1-2 (3), 2-3 (4), 3-4 (2). Every one of those edges costs at most 7, so 1-4 would only add a dearer way round a loop. Skip it.
Edge 0-2 costs 8, but the tree already joins 0 to 2 through 0-1 (5), 1-2 (3). Every one of those edges costs at most 8, so 0-2 would only add a dearer way round a loop. Skip it.
The finished tree costs 23. Each skipped edge lost to a path of cheaper or equal edges, so nothing cheaper was thrown away.

Kruskal's algorithm builds the tree edge by edge. Each step below stops at an edge it skips, with the tree built so far marked. A skipped edge's ends are already joined by accepted edges, so it would close a cycle.
Edge 0-2 costs 8, but the tree already joins 0 to 2 through 0-1 (5), 1-2 (3). Every one of those edges costs at most 8, so 0-2 would only add a dearer way round a loop. Skip it.
Edge 3-5 costs 9, but the tree already joins 3 to 5 through 3-4 (2), 4-5 (6). Every one of those edges costs at most 9, so 3-5 would only add a dearer way round a loop. Skip it.
The forest has 4 edges and cannot be completed: some cities are cut off, so there is no spanning tree and the answer is -1.
